title: Social media has become a central youth environment where attention, learning, identity, inequality, and policy collide
source_unit: OECD Digital Economy Papers No. 385, Growing up in the social media age
geography: OECD countries, primarily 15-year-olds and 2022 PISA-linked digital-leisure, academic, and creative-thinking evidence

denominator.unit: OECD 15-year-old population represented in the report's cross-country analysis

weekly_social_media_time.unit: approximately hours per week spent on social media on average

daily_browsing.unit: percent reporting browsing social media daily

daily_communicating_sharing.unit: percent reporting communicating or sharing digital content daily

cross_country_range.value: under 26 to over 45 hours per week

observations.method: OECD analysis of PISA 2022 digital-leisure measures and literature on social media use among young people.
observations.uncertainty: Reported time is survey-based and does not establish platform-specific exposure, content quality, multitasking, or causal effects on learning or well-being.
observations.subgroup: 15-year-olds across OECD countries, with differences by country, sex, and socio-economic background.
observations.counterinterpretation: High use can include connection, information, play, creativity, and peer support; time alone does not distinguish beneficial from harmful activity.

observations.period: 2022 PISA-linked evidence; sex and socio-economic differences

denominator.unit: OECD 15-year-old students with reported digital-leisure patterns

girls_social_media_time.unit: average hours per week for girls

boys_social_media_time.unit: average hours per week for boys

low_ses_difference_girls.unit: additional average weekly hours reported by girls in the lowest socio-economic quartile compared with the highest quartile

low_ses_difference_boys.unit: additional average weekly hours reported by boys in the lowest socio-economic quartile compared with the highest quartile

observations.method: OECD subgroup comparisons of reported digital leisure by sex and socio-economic background.
observations.uncertainty: Subgroup gaps are descriptive associations; they do not establish whether social media causes the differences or whether other time, family, school, or neighborhood conditions explain them.
observations.subgroup: Girls and boys, lower- and higher-socio-economic-background students, and students in different OECD education systems.
observations.counterinterpretation: Higher use among disadvantaged students may reflect social connection or limited alternatives, while lower use may reflect unequal access or different reporting rather than lower exposure to risk.

observations.period: 2022 PISA-linked evidence; academic performance and creative thinking

denominator.unit: OECD student associations analyzed using reported social-media activity and PISA outcomes

academic_pattern.value: moderate social-media use is associated with higher test scores, while excessive use is associated with falling academic performance

creative_thinking_pattern.value: creative-thinking scores peak at moderate levels of browsing, roughly one to three hours per day

communication_threshold_pattern.value: more than one hour of weekday or weekend communication/sharing is associated with declining measured creative-thinking scores

observations.method: OECD analysis of associations between digital-leisure behavior and PISA academic and creative-thinking outcomes.
observations.uncertainty: These are observational associations and may reflect reverse causality, selection, omitted variables, content differences, or reporting error; they are not dose-response causal estimates.
observations.subgroup: 15-year-old students with different levels and types of browsing, communication, sharing, and gaming activity.
observations.counterinterpretation: The relationship may be non-linear and activity-specific: moderate use can support creativity or connection, while intensive or distracting use can coincide with poorer outcomes.

observations.period: 2026 policy review; social-media governance for young people

denominator.unit: OECD review of policy approaches to young people's social-media use

policy_direction.value: mobile-phone restrictions in schools and dedicated social-media laws or minimum-age rules are gaining policy attention

implementation_challenge.value: school device restrictions have become more common but implementation is difficult

policy_balance.value: policy must protect against risks while safeguarding expression, privacy, innovation, and fair competition

observations.method: OECD review of research and national/subnational policy approaches to young people's social-media use.
observations.uncertainty: Policy adoption does not establish enforcement, compliance, effectiveness, or equal impact; restrictions can shift activity across platforms or into less visible settings.
observations.subgroup: Young people, families, educators, schools, platforms, regulators, and communities with different digital access and safety conditions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Well-designed digital literacy, platform accountability, safer product design, and supportive school practice may complement or outperform blanket restrictions in some contexts.

related_sources.claim: OECD citation and persistent identifier for Digital Economy Papers No. 385.
UNICEF child-rights and agency evidence provides a complementary youth voice and protection frame.

boundary: This record adds a youth digital-life route linking social-media time, attention, communication, creativity, academic performance, gender, socio-economic inequality, well-being, school practice, and platform regulation. It is a comparative publication-level synthesis using aggregate and survey-linked evidence, not respondent-level histories, clinical mental-health data, platform telemetry, causal effects, or proof that a specific restriction improves outcomes.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: OECD full report and executive-summary sections were reviewed for youth-use levels, subgroup differences, academic and creative-thinking associations, policy approaches, and causal-boundary language.
